title: Masterclass 24
description: Phase 3 polishing and optional advanced challenges; universal timbre work and final aural-recall verification assignment.

practices.title: Comments
practices.text: Source review: text_supported_audio_unverified. Source instructions and app adaptations are separated in Practice info / source. Optional practices are excluded from mastery. Manual logs do not establish correctness. See docs/CLASSES_22_24.md.

practices.title: Solo aural recall with a selected target
practices.description: Write all twelve tone names on cards and draw one from a hat/box, or point to a piano key without playing it. Sing the selected pitch before playing it; play to check. For an error, compare the sung pitch with the intended pitch live, then gently think of each color inwardly. Do not strain to imagine vivid colors.

info.purpose: Learn the solo recall procedure, live/mental error comparison, and non-straining approach.
info.source_audio: David Lucas Burge - Master Class 24 - The Perfect Pitch Ear Training SuperCourse [YaPVo0VHGs8].mp3

source_windows.description: Select a tone using cards or an unplayed piano key, sing before sounding it, then compare errors.
Compare wrong and intended pitch colors inwardly after hearing them live.
Recall gently and correct errors without straining the imagination.

info.skill: recall a named pitch before hearing it
source_instructions: Write all twelve tone names on cards and draw one from a hat/box, or point to a piano key without playing it.
Sing the selected pitch before playing it; play to check.
For an error, compare the sung pitch with the intended pitch live, then gently think of each color inwardly.
Do not strain to imagine vivid colors.

target_options: Cards naming all twelve tones in a hat or box

info.presentation: Choose a target without sounding it first; G and A-flat are explanatory examples.
info.response: Sing the target from memory, then check against the instrument.
info.correction: Listen to the wrong and correct pitches, then easily recall their contrasting feelings mentally.

evidence.quote: oral recall by myself all right now this advanced stage of perfect pitch where you can just sing any
tone at will what you can do by yourself you don't even need a partner for this
if you have color discrimination and you can even do this if you don't have color
discrimination because remember these levels all grow up simultaneously but it
works best when you've already developed your color discrimination just write out
the notes A, Bb, B, C, C sharp, D, all of the 12 tones on a card and put them in a hat
or put them in a box and just pick out one. Or just reach out to your piano and point
to one. You're not looking and just point to this G here. And then sing that G before
you play it. Then play it and see if you were right. And if you're not, see where you were
were wrong. If you sang a wrong note, if you sang an A-flat, then listen to the color of
the A-flat and then listen to the color of the G. But you have to go further than this.
Then you have to mentally think of the color of the A-flat and mentally think of the color
of the G. It's easier to hear the pitch colors live. Hear that the A-flat is kind of a soft
soft quality, and the G is a little different. But then when you think of it mentally and
you kind of hear it inwardly, inside your own mind, the difference between those colors,
then this is where the aural recall develops. We have to have heard the colors live quite
nicely before then we can start to remember them, because memory is always a little bit
more vague than the actual experience itself, of course.
Now, one thing we don't do is we don't strain our minds
by trying to imagine these colors
and clearly hearing the difference in the mind.
No, no, this is going to give a headache.
What we do is we just gently allow ourselves
to think of these colors just very easily.
The aural recall will grow naturally.
The more times you try to remember a pitch,
the more the mind will start to click into gear
with producing that pitch for you.
If you always know an A every time you hear it,
It's not much of a step to be able to think up that A by yourself.
So you just keep trying to think it up, and when you get it wrong, you correct that error.
But remember, we always do it easily. We never strain doing this.
Very, very important point.

prerequisites: Color discrimination is recommended for best results, but the source permits trying earlier.
uncertainties: No tuning tolerance, vocal range, or quota is specified for this preparatory version.

Naming is an app response choice where the source leaves response unspecified; help is not verification credit.

practices.title: Missing tone in a scale
practices.description: Use a whole C-major scale with one tone omitted. Find its root and mentally climb the scale to find the absent tone. Whole-tone scales are another option. Work live rather than attempting to decode the recorded example.

info.purpose: Check the optional live missing-scale-tone challenge and its listening strategy.
info.source_audio: David Lucas Burge - Master Class 24 - The Perfect Pitch Ear Training SuperCourse [YaPVo0VHGs8].mp3

source_windows.description: Live C-major scale with one omitted tone: find the root and climb mentally to the gap; do not decode the recording as a pitch test.
Whole-tone scales are another optional version, with A-sharp as a spoken omission example.

audience: advanced learners with a partner or live chord presentation
source_instructions: Use a whole C-major scale with one tone omitted.
Find its root and mentally climb the scale to find the absent tone.
Whole-tone scales are another option.
Work live rather than attempting to decode the recorded example.
info.presentation: Scale tones presented as a live combined sound with one omitted; G and A-sharp are example omissions, not fixed requirements.

evidence.quote: school. We do things like maybe take an entire C major scale, except we're leaving one tone
out. Don't try to hear this on this CD or this tape that you're listening to because
this is very hard to hear this. You have to kind of be live with this. But I've got C,
C, D, E, F, and I've skipped G, and then I've got A, B, and C. So what you have to do is
you have to listen very carefully and find the root of all those tones, which is the
C, and then climb up in your mind's ear until you don't hear one of the tones.
The G is missing, and that is your challenge there, to find the missing tone.
You can do this with whole tone scales as well.
I've got a whole tone scale, except I've left out the A sharp.
You just have to work with these.
You may think they're impossible.
They're not impossible.

implementation_decisions: Treat this as an optional ear teaser, not a required progression gate.
uncertainties: Octave/voicing details beyond the spoken C-major example are not specified.
Spoken note labels do not verify the recording’s pitches.
app_adaptations: Optional generated C-major missing-tone teaser: seven unique scale notes from root MIDI60, one omitted, six sounded simultaneously. No octave-doubled root. This app voicing is not the exact source C-to-C example or verified recorded audio. Omission varies; G is only a source example. No success quota or note-help controls.

practices.title: Missing tone in a chromatic cluster
practices.description: Present chromatic tones as one cluster with one tone left out. Listen for the bottom and top tones, then climb chromatically inward to locate the omission. Take time to listen rather than expecting a quick answer.

info.purpose: Check the chromatic-cluster challenge and the slow boundary-to-interior listening method.
info.source_audio: David Lucas Burge - Master Class 24 - The Perfect Pitch Ear Training SuperCourse [YaPVo0VHGs8].mp3

source_windows.description: Present one chromatic cluster with a missing tone; find the bottom and take time.
Find the top, climb chromatically, and locate the omission; narrated note names are examples, not verified pitches.

audience: advanced learners with a partner or live chord presentation
info.skill: auditory separation in a dissonant cluster
source_instructions: Present chromatic tones as one cluster with one tone left out.
Listen for the bottom and top tones, then climb chromatically inward to locate the omission.
Take time to listen rather than expecting a quick answer.
info.presentation: Simultaneous chromatic cluster; the narrated C-to-A cluster missing F is an example.

evidence.quote: This is one of the things that Richard and I used to like to do.
You take chromatic tones in one big cluster, but I'm leaving out one of the tones.
Now, the way I would always get this when we would do this together, I would first listen
for the bottom tone.
And don't think you're going to do this quickly.
You have to sit there and listen a little bit to get this.
And you hear that the bottom tone is C. And then you find the top tone, A. Then you have
have to climb chromatically C-sharp, D, E-flat, E, and then you don't hear the F, so that's
the one that's missing because we do have F-sharp, G, A-flat, and A. This is a real
challenge because all the tones are so dissonant, they're clashing with each other, that it's
sometimes difficult to get in there and find, well, which tone is not there? But these are
really fun drills to do to sharpen your ear and enliven it even more. There's no end to ear

implementation_decisions: Optional challenge; do not encode the example as the sole valid cluster.
uncertainties: No success quota or correction routine is supplied.
app_adaptations: Optional generated cluster uses MIDI60 through MIDI72 inclusive, with exactly one INTERIOR MIDI note omitted; both bounds always sound. Bounds and interior-only omission are explicit app choices to support boundary listening, not source requirements. Source endpoints/register are not established as a general rule; its narrated C-to-A/F example is not an audio-verified bank. No success quota or note-help controls.

practices.title: Tune the guitar A string from pitch feeling
practices.description: Tune the A string by finding where A is. After settling on A, check with a tuning fork or tuner. Use an actual guitar: tune the A string from remembered pitch, settle on your choice, then check with a tuning fork or tuner. The app does not tune, measure cents or grade this action.

info.purpose: Check the tune-first, verify-afterward guitar exercise for refined pitch judgment.
info.source_audio: David Lucas Burge - Master Class 24 - The Perfect Pitch Ear Training SuperCourse [YaPVo0VHGs8].mp3

source_windows.description: Find A by tuning the A string, then check with a tuning fork or tuner; no numerical tolerance is stated.

source_instructions: Tune the A string by finding where A is.
After settling on A, check with a tuning fork or tuner.
info.presentation: Tune before consulting the external check.
info.response: Set the string to the remembered A, then check how close it is.

evidence.quote: always improve yourself more, if you want. For example, we can develop our refined color
discrimination. You can listen very carefully to see if a tone is sharp or flat. Guitarists,
you can go to an A string and tune it.
Find where the A is.
And once you settle on your A,
check it with a tuning fork or a tuner
to see if you have hit the A pretty closely.
This will encourage your refined color discrimination,
the ability to judge if the tone is sharp or flat.

uncertainties: No cents tolerance, repetition count, or explicit correction sequence is given.
app_adaptations: Use an actual guitar: tune the A string from remembered pitch, settle on your choice, then check with a tuning fork or tuner. The app does not tune, measure cents or grade this action. Manual session logging is not an assessment or proof of mastery; no generated notes, microphone assessment, cents tolerance, timing or repetition quota is implied.
